passage:
A moon or planet is said to be tidally locked when it rotates on its axis in exactly the time it takes to complete one orbit around its primary, with the result that it keeps the same face turned toward that body at all times. The Earth's Moon is the familiar example: the side we see from Earth is always the same side, and the so-called far side was first photographed only in 1959, by a Soviet spacecraft that passed behind it. Tidal locking is not an exotic accident; it is the predictable endpoint of a process that operates, to some degree, on every orbiting pair.

The mechanism is straightforward. Any body that is not perfectly rigid deforms slightly in response to the gravitational pull of its neighbor, bulging toward the neighbor and, by a more subtle effect, on the side facing away as well. If the deforming body rotates faster than it orbits, each bulge is carried ahead of the line connecting the two centers before the body can reshape itself, and the neighbor's gravity then pulls back on the leading bulge. This drag slowly removes rotational energy. Over time, the spin rate falls until it matches the orbital period, at which point the bulges sit on the line between the two centers and the braking torque disappears.

How long this takes depends strongly on a few variables. Smaller separations make the bulges larger and the braking more severe, so close-in bodies lock first. Bodies with less internal stiffness also lock faster, because they deform more readily and generate larger bulges in response to the same pull. For the Earth-Moon system, calculations indicate that the Moon became locked within roughly a few tens of millions of years, a brief interval on a solar-system timescale. Earth itself is being slowed by the Moon, but the process is far slower because Earth is much more massive, and full locking will not occur before the Sun's eventual expansion overtakes the system.

One implication of the mechanism is often overlooked. Because tidal locking removes rotational energy, a tidally locked body has generally lost the internal circulation that a faster spin would have driven, and its climate, if it has an atmosphere, becomes organized around a permanent day side and a permanent night side rather than around a daily cycle. Astronomers studying planets that orbit close to small, cool stars now routinely assume such planets are locked, and recent models of their atmospheres take the resulting asymmetry as a starting point rather than a complication.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tidal locking is a predictable physical process in which a rotating body's spin is gradually brought into step with its orbital period, and its effects extend to the climates of locked planets.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the Moon became tidally locked to Earth within a few tens of millions of years, tidal locking must be regarded as an unusually rapid astronomical process.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Planets that orbit close to small, cool stars are almost certainly tidally locked and therefore have atmospheres organized around a permanent day side and a permanent night side.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The far side of the Moon was unknown to scientists until a Soviet spacecraft photographed it in 1959, demonstrating how little had been known about tidal locking at that time.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tidal locking results from the deformation of orbiting bodies and is impossible in any system whose members are perfectly rigid.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 introduces locking as the endpoint of a general process; paragraphs 2 and 3 explain the mechanism and how quickly it operates; paragraph 4 extends the picture to climate on locked planets. Choice A captures both the mechanism and its broader implication.
explanations.B: Paragraph-restatement: captures a specific estimate from paragraph 3, not the overall thesis.
explanations.C: Too narrow: the close-in-exoplanet case is one implication in the last paragraph, not the main point.
explanations.D: Too narrow / illustrative-example: the 1959 photograph is a supporting detail in paragraph 1.
explanations.E: Too-strong: the passage says no body is perfectly rigid but does not claim locking would be impossible in a purely hypothetical rigid pair as its main thesis.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A phenomenon is defined with an example, its mechanism is explained, the variables governing its rate are identified, and a broader implication is drawn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Two competing accounts of a phenomenon are described, and evidence is offered that supports the second over the first.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A historical puzzle is introduced, an early hypothesis is rejected, and a newer hypothesis is defended.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An observation is reported, its sources of uncertainty are catalogued, and the reader is warned against overinterpreting it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A general principle is stated, illustrated with a counterexample, and then abandoned in favor of a more modest claim.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines tidal locking and gives the Moon as the canonical case; paragraph 2 explains the bulge-and-drag mechanism; paragraph 3 identifies the variables that control how fast locking occurs; paragraph 4 draws the climate implication.
explanations.B: Mis-sequencing: no competing accounts are set against one another.
explanations.D: Wrong grain / wrong tone: the passage is explanatory, not a catalogue of uncertainties.
explanations.E: Opposite: the principle is not abandoned; it is extended in the final paragraph.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the rotational braking torque responsible for tidal locking disappears when

choices.label: A
choices.text: the deforming body has become perfectly rigid and can no longer form bulges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: the two bodies have drifted far enough apart that their mutual gravitational pull is negligible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the deforming body's spin rate has fallen into step with its orbital period, so that its bulges lie on the line connecting the two centers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: the orbital period of the pair has become long enough that the bulges can no longer be carried ahead of the connecting line.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the central body has itself begun to rotate at the same rate as its companion.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 states that as the spin rate falls to match the orbital period, 'the bulges sit on the line between the two centers and the braking torque disappears.'
explanations.A: Altered premise: the passage denies that any real body is perfectly rigid; this is not what ends the torque.
explanations.B: Outside scope: the passage does not invoke orbital separation becoming negligible.
explanations.D: Plausible-world fact: not stated; the relevant comparison is spin versus orbit, not orbital period in isolation.
explanations.E: The passage discusses the central body's rotation only briefly and does not tie the torque's disappearance to it.

questions.questionStem: The passage states that Earth's full tidal locking to the Moon

choices.label: A
choices.text: has effectively already occurred, though the final adjustment remains to be measured.

choices.label: B
choices.text: is proceeding, but will not be completed before the Sun's eventual expansion overtakes the system.

choices.label: C
choices.text: is prevented by Earth's internal circulation, which continually restores its rotational energy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: will occur within roughly a few tens of millions of years, on the same timescale as the Moon's locking.

choices.label: E
choices.text: cannot occur because Earth is more massive than the Moon.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says Earth 'is being slowed by the Moon, but the process is far slower... and full locking will not occur before the Sun's eventual expansion overtakes the system.'
explanations.A: The passage says the process is slow, not that it has effectively occurred.
explanations.C: Wrong causation: internal circulation is tied to tidally locked bodies in paragraph 4, not to why Earth has not yet locked.
explanations.D: Wrong figure: the few-tens-of-millions estimate refers to the Moon's locking, not Earth's.
explanations.E: Too-strong: the passage says the process is slow because Earth is more massive, not that locking is impossible.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests which one of the following about two small moons identical in size and composition but orbiting the same planet at different distances?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The more distant moon, other things being equal, will become tidally locked sooner than the closer moon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The closer moon, other things being equal, will become tidally locked sooner than the more distant moon.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither moon will ever become tidally locked unless it has an atmosphere.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moons will become tidally locked at the same time, since composition determines the rate of locking.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tidal locking applies only to moons that are larger than their primary, and so the scenario cannot arise.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says smaller separations produce larger bulges and more severe braking, so 'close-in bodies lock first.' For two otherwise identical moons, the closer one locks sooner.
explanations.A: Direction-reversed: the passage says close-in bodies lock first.
explanations.C: Outside scope: atmospheres are discussed only as a consequence of locking, not as a prerequisite for it.
explanations.D: Ignores separation: composition is only one of several variables the passage identifies.
explanations.E: The passage never restricts locking to moons larger than their primary; the usual case is the reverse.

questions.questionStem: The author's mention of the 1959 Soviet photograph of the far side of the Moon functions in the passage primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate what it means for a body to keep the same face turned toward its primary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish that scientific understanding of tidal locking dates only to the late 1950s.

choices.label: C
choices.text: provide historical evidence that contradicts an earlier theory of the Moon's rotation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: contrast human observation of the Moon with observation of exoplanets.

choices.label: E
choices.text: explain why tidal locking is a faster process than had previously been assumed.

explanations.correct: The reference comes immediately after the sentence describing how a locked body keeps the same face toward its primary; the photograph is offered to make that abstract definition concrete.
explanations.B: Accurate-content-wrong-function: the passage doesn't use the date to make a claim about when tidal locking began to be understood.
explanations.C: No earlier theory of lunar rotation is under discussion.
explanations.D: Plausible-but-unused: the contrast with exoplanets appears in paragraph 4, not in connection with the 1959 photograph.
explanations.E: Unsupported: the passage does not compare prior and current estimates of locking speed.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the mechanism of tidal locking described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A spinning top slows and eventually stops because friction between its tip and the floor removes rotational energy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A flexible rubber ball, repeatedly squeezed out of round as it rolls past a strong magnet, loses speed because each deformation is pulled backward by the magnet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A ship at anchor rocks with the tide but does not drift, because its anchor chain holds it in place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pendulum eventually comes to rest as air resistance steadily removes energy at the bottom of each swing.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A dropped ball bounces lower each time because each collision with the floor dissipates some of its energy as heat.

explanations.correct: The passage's mechanism has three load-bearing parts: (i) a deformable body, (ii) a deformation pulled ahead of where the external pull would like it, and (iii) that external pull dragging the deformation back, which slowly removes energy. B preserves all three.
explanations.A: Surface-similarity: friction slows a rotation, but there is no deformation being pulled back by the external body.
explanations.C: The chain here provides a restoring force, not a braking drag from a misaligned deformation.
explanations.D: Air resistance is undirected drag; there is no deformation carried ahead of an external attractor.
explanations.E: Energy is lost to heat at each collision, but the mechanism is not the misalignment of a deformation relative to an attracting body.

passage:
In many lakes at high latitudes, the sediment that settles on the bottom each year is not uniform but instead forms two thin bands of contrasting color and texture. These paired bands are called varves (a term borrowed from the Swedish word for 'turn' or 'layer'), and where conditions are right they accumulate one pair per year, much as a tree adds one ring per growing season. A careful count of varves in a suitable lake bed can therefore yield a calendar of past years, sometimes reaching back many thousands of seasons.

The formation of a varve depends on the lake's annual rhythm. During the spring melt, streams deliver a burst of suspended sediment, and the coarser particles settle first, forming a relatively pale, sandy layer on the lake bottom. As the water warms and biological activity peaks through summer, finer particles and organic matter remain in suspension. When the lake cools in autumn and, in many cases, freezes over in winter, this finer material finally settles, producing a darker, clay-rich layer above the pale one. A single pair — pale below, dark above — marks one full year.

Not all lakes preserve varves. The record depends on the absence of mixing: if currents, burrowing organisms, or seasonal overturn stir the lake bed, the delicate layers are destroyed. For that reason, well-preserved varves tend to be found in lakes that are deep, cold, and chemically stratified, so that oxygen does not reach the bottom and little lives there to disturb the sediment. A few such lakes have yielded continuous records spanning more than ten thousand years, and in some cases the individual layers can be matched across widely separated basins, suggesting that the sediment supply is responding to a regional, rather than purely local, climate.

Because each varve corresponds to a single year, thickness variations can be read with unusual directness. A thick pale band typically indicates a vigorous spring melt, and a sequence of thick pairs suggests a run of wet or warm years. Geologists combine such readings with other archives — tree rings, ice cores, and pollen records — to reconstruct past climates. Varves do not by themselves settle any large question about long-term climate change, but they offer one of the few records that is annually resolved and directly datable, and for that reason they remain a reference against which other, less precise archives are frequently checked.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Varves, annually paired sediment layers that form in certain undisturbed lakes, provide a directly datable year-by-year archive that is valuable for reconstructing past climates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because varves are disturbed by burrowing organisms and seasonal overturn in most lakes, they can rarely be used to reconstruct past climates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tree rings, ice cores, and pollen records are generally less reliable than varves and have therefore been supplanted by them in reconstructions of past climates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A thick pale band in a varve sequence invariably indicates a year of heavy spring runoff and relatively warm summer temperatures.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varves demonstrate that long-term regional climate change has occurred across widely separated lake basins over the past ten thousand years.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 defines varves and their calendar-like nature; paragraphs 2 and 3 explain how they form and why some lakes preserve them; paragraph 4 describes their use in reconstructing past climates. Choice A integrates these strands.
explanations.B: Paragraph-restatement / opposite: paragraph 3 mentions disturbance as a limitation but emphasizes that well-preserved records do exist.
explanations.C: Too strong: the passage says varves are checked against other archives, not that they have supplanted them.
explanations.D: Too narrow / too strong: captures a detail from paragraph 4 and overstates it with 'invariably.'
explanations.E: Opposite of author's hedge: the passage explicitly says varves 'do not by themselves settle any large question about long-term climate change.'

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward the use of varves in reconstructing past climates can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of varves as the single most authoritative climate archive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: cautious approval that acknowledges both their value and their limits.

choices.label: C
choices.text: skeptical dismissal grounded in the fragility of the sedimentary record.

choices.label: D
choices.text: impartial neutrality, neither endorsing nor criticizing their use.

choices.label: E
choices.text: anxious pessimism about the prospects for reliable reconstruction of past climates in general.

explanations.correct: The author describes varves as an unusually direct annual record that remains 'a reference against which other, less precise archives are frequently checked,' while also noting that they 'do not by themselves settle any large question' about long-term climate. That is cautious approval.
explanations.A: Too-strong: the author does not claim varves are the single most authoritative archive.
explanations.C: Opposite-tone: the author treats varves as valuable.
explanations.D: The author's positive evaluation (calling them a reference standard) is explicit.
explanations.E: No anxious or pessimistic language about climate reconstruction appears.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, the darker, finer-grained layer of a varve pair is deposited primarily

choices.label: A
choices.text: during the initial burst of spring runoff, when streams are carrying the greatest sediment load.

choices.label: B
choices.text: in late summer, when biological activity in the lake is at its peak.

choices.label: C
choices.text: in autumn and winter, when the lake cools and fine particles and organic matter finally settle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: only in lakes whose bottoms are regularly disturbed by burrowing organisms.

choices.label: E
choices.text: at irregular intervals that do not correspond to any particular season.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 says that when the lake cools in autumn and in many cases freezes in winter, 'this finer material finally settles, producing a darker, clay-rich layer above the pale one.'
explanations.A: Wrong sentence: spring runoff produces the pale, coarser layer.
explanations.B: Wrong sentence: during peak summer activity, the fine material remains in suspension.
explanations.D: Direction-reversed: burrowing organisms destroy varves rather than forming them.
explanations.E: Altered premise: the passage ties each varve to a specific annual cycle.

questions.questionStem: The passage identifies which one of the following as a feature of lakes especially likely to preserve varves?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A warm surface layer that promotes rapid biological activity year-round.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Abundant bottom-dwelling organisms whose burrows mark successive years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chemical stratification that keeps oxygen from reaching the lake bottom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Frequent seasonal overturn that mixes deep water with surface water.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A shallow basin whose sediment is regularly resuspended by currents.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 states that well-preserved varves tend to occur in lakes that are 'deep, cold, and chemically stratified, so that oxygen does not reach the bottom and little lives there to disturb the sediment.'
explanations.A: Altered premise: the passage emphasizes cold, stratified lakes rather than warm surface waters.
explanations.B: Opposite: burrowing organisms are said to destroy varves, not preserve them.
explanations.D: Opposite: the passage lists seasonal overturn as a disturbance that destroys varves.
explanations.E: Opposite: resuspension by currents is explicitly destructive of varve layering.

questions.questionStem: It can most reasonably be inferred from the passage that if geologists examining a well-preserved varve sequence find a run of unusually thick pale bands across several consecutive years, they would most likely conclude that during those years

choices.label: A
choices.text: the lake was repeatedly disturbed by burrowing organisms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: spring melt was especially vigorous, delivering more suspended sediment than usual.

choices.label: C
choices.text: the lake experienced exceptionally cold winters that suppressed biological activity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: organic matter made up a larger-than-usual share of the sediment reaching the lake bottom.

choices.label: E
choices.text: the lake's chemical stratification temporarily broke down.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 4 says 'a thick pale band typically indicates a vigorous spring melt, and a sequence of thick pairs suggests a run of wet or warm years.' A run of thick pale bands therefore supports the vigorous-melt inference.
explanations.A: Direction-reversed: burrowing would disturb, not thicken, the layers.
explanations.C: The passage connects thick pale bands to melt intensity, not to winter biological activity.
explanations.D: Outside scope: organic matter contributes mainly to the darker layer in the passage's model.
explanations.E: Breakdown of stratification would degrade the record, not produce thick pale bands.

questions.questionStem: The author's comparison of varves to tree rings in paragraph 1 serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: give the reader a familiar image of a yearly layered record against which the novel concept of varves can be understood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: suggest that the same biological processes responsible for tree rings also drive the formation of varves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: establish that varves are more reliable than tree rings for reconstructing past climates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: imply that tree rings are too short in record length to be useful for climate research.

choices.label: E
choices.text: argue that annual layered records should be preferred to any nonlayered archive.

explanations.correct: The comparison appears as varves are introduced, and functions as an orienting analogy: one pair per year, one ring per growing season. It anchors the new idea in a familiar one.
explanations.B: The analogy is structural, not claimed to share biological mechanism.
explanations.C: No such reliability ranking is asserted in paragraph 1; paragraph 4 treats them as complementary.
explanations.D: The passage does not say tree-ring records are too short.
explanations.E: The argumentative claim about preferring layered records is not advanced by the analogy.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most strengthen the claim that a given lake's sediment record is responding to regional rather than purely local climate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lake is deeper and colder than most neighboring lakes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thickness pattern of the lake's varves over a several-century interval closely matches the varve-thickness pattern in lakes in distant basins over the same interval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lake is fed by a single stream whose watershed lies entirely within a few kilometers of the lake.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Individual varve pairs in the lake are unusually thick compared with those in other known varved lakes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The lake's bottom sediments contain abundant organic matter from local aquatic plants.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 says that matching individual layers across widely separated basins suggests a regional rather than purely local driver. A multi-century thickness match with distant basins is exactly that kind of evidence.
explanations.A: Speaks to preservation conditions, not to whether the climate signal is regional.
explanations.C: If anything, weakens: a purely local watershed favors a local explanation.
explanations.D: Thickness compared to other lakes does not show that the same climate signal is acting across them.
explanations.E: Organic content from local plants has no bearing on regional-versus-local climate inference.
